title: LLM Ops handyman jotter — quick reads + micro experiments
content:
Purpose: keep short cognitive snapshots of recent papers/blogs/workshop snippets and immediate micro-experiments I want to run. Not polished — rapid-fire notes and TODOs for the week.

Highlights (fast):
- Paper: "Efficient KV Compression for Long Contexts" — key idea: blockwise lossy compression of KV with rehydration when divergence detected. Promising tradeoff for cost-limited dedicated tiers.
- Blog: "Adaptive Batching for Low-latency Inference" — heuristics for combining deadline-aware batching with burst-suppression. Useful for our edge bursts.
- Workshop: EdgeOps microtalk — consensus: small per-request amortization wins when combined with prefix caching and opportunistic prefetch.

Short summaries and my reading impressions:
1) Efficient KV Compression for Long Contexts (link: arxiv.org/abs/3401.12345)
   - Core: quantize / project KV blocks into 8-16 byte summaries per token-range + light decoder to reconstruct during forward pass.
   - Good when: sequence has long repeated context or strong topical locality.
   - Worries: reconstruction cost spikes for random-access patterns; tricky to integrate with GPU kernels.
   - Ops idea: run a sim on our trace logs to compute compressibility score per tenant (metric: fraction of tokens that can be stored at 0.5x bytes with <1% perplexity delta).
   - Quick TODO: write a parser to sample 1M requests from prod traces and compute block-wise entropy (3h).

2) Adaptive Batching for Low-latency Inference (engineering blog)
   - Key takeaways: deadline buckets + probabilistic merge policy outperforms fixed-time windows for p95 latency SLOs.
   - Implementation notes: maintain small per-core fibrillation queue; tune merge threshold by tail-latency target rather than throughput.
   - Ops experiment: toggle merge policy in canary worker pool (dedicated pool) for 2h and compare token/sec and p95. Hypothesis: p95 down 15% at <5% throughput loss.

3) Workshop notes: EdgeOps microtalks
   - Pre-warm nets for high-traffic routes + prefix caching is low effort, high impact.
   - Acceptable fallback: if prefix cache miss and model busy, return early-best-effort chunk from cached shorter-context variant. Implement fallback routing in ~half-day prototype.

Micro-experiments to run (prioritized):
A) Compressibility scan on traces (Priority: high)
   - Steps: sample traces -> compute per-16k token block entropy -> measure redundancy windows -> output distribution for top 20 tenants.
   - Success signal: >30% bytes reducible at <1.5% LM-score delta for at least 5 tenants.

B) Canary adaptive-batch merge policy (Priority: medium)
   - Steps: instrument worker pool with new merge policy flag; run hour-long windows in low-traffic zone; capture p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, CPU/GPU utilization.
   - Snippet for merge policy config (pseudo):
     merge_window_ms: 6
     merge_priority_score: lambda(q_len, deadline) -> q_len / max(1, remaining_deadline_ms)

C) Fallback-to-shorter-model prototype (Priority: medium-low)
   - Idea: route to smaller context-length model when prefix cache miss and queue depth > threshold. Measure impact on hallucination rate and latency.

Notes-to-self (rough):
- Don't conflate 'compressibility' with 'compressibility that helps GPU memory pressure' — need a second metric that models GPU memory layout (KV shard boundary awareness).
- Talk to infra team re: trace access; sampling aggregator exists (see JIRA-OPS-1173) but needs permission for tenant-level analysis.
- Add an internal eval: take compressed/rehydrated contexts and run 100 curated prompts used in Optimize tests. Compute MAU-level regression signals.

Snippets / quick commands to run locally:
- Trace sampling (one-liner):
  python infra/tools/sample_traces.py --src gs://redwood-prod/traces/2024/ --out local-samples/ --count 100000 --seed 42

- Toy KV-block entropy (very rough):
  from collections import Counter
  def block_entropy(tokens):
      c = Counter(tokens)
      import math
      n = sum(c.values())
      return -sum((v/n) * math.log2(v/n) for v in c.values())

Open questions / risks:
- How well does block compression interact with KV-sharding across GPUs? Could cause uneven memory and QoS hotspots.
- If we rehydrate lazily, tail latency could spike unpredictably for some requests — need cap on rehydration CPU/GPU budget per shard.
- Regulatory/data: compressing context blobs could change storage classification — sync with security/legal before storing compressed user contexts.

Meeting actions (who):
- (Me) Draft analysis plan and ask infra for sampling permission (by 2034-03-14).
- (Ravi) Quick check if we have existing kernel hooks to do lightweight rehydration (by 2034-03-15).
- (Maya) Help author the eval set for compressed-context quality checks (by 2034-03-16).

One-line landing plan (if compressibility looks good):
1) Proof-of-concept offline scan -> 2) integrate a compress/rehydrate shim in the serving runtime behind a feature flag -> 3) small canary for low-traffic tenants -> 4) monitor p95/p99 and quality regressions -> 5) iterate on block-size/rehydration heuristics.

Random thoughts (brain dump):
- Could use an index of 'hot windows' within long contexts (like attention hotspots) instead of uniform blocks — maybe guided by gradients or importance sampling.
- Combination idea: compress infrequent windows and keep recent windows exact. Warmup policy could prefetch for returning users.

Endnotes: short, messy, useful. Will trim if turning into a Confluence write-up.
